entityDossier.whatItIs: AATIP is the unclassified nickname attached to a Defense Intelligence Agency effort that ran on congressional earmarks from FY2008 through roughly 2012, executed under contract by Bigelow Aerospace Advanced Space Studies LLC (BAASS) of North Las Vegas. Primary documents show the name used in at least three incompatible ways: as the DIA contract line (Advanced Aerospace Threat and Identification Program), as the internal DIA program office designation (AAWSAP, the Advanced Aerospace Weapon System Applications Program), and as a later OUSD(I) activity that Luis Elizondo says he ran and that DoD public affairs says never officially existed. The naming collision is not trivia; it is the seam along which the whole custody question runs.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: AATIP is the only publicly documented instance in which a sitting Senate Majority Leader wrote to a Deputy Secretary of Defense asking for a Restricted SAP with a Bigoted Access List to protect, in his own words, "the methodology used to identify, acquire, study, and engineer the advanced technologies associated with AATIP." Acquire and engineer are custody and reverse-engineering verbs, and Reid put them in a signed letter dated 24 June 2009 to William Lynn III. DIA's own December 2010 info memo from LTG Ronald Burgess to USD(AT&L) confirms the SAP request, confirms DIA refused it in November 2009 for lack of classification grounds, and then confirms Burgess told Reid the work "could be transitioned to another agency or component better suited to oversee the project." That single sentence is the hinge: it is DIA, in writing, describing the handoff that becomes KONA BLUE eighteen months later. Everything the Pentagon has said since 2017 about AATIP has been an argument about the name rather than a denial of the paper trail, and the paper trail is signed by Reid, Lynn, Burgess and Maples.
entityDossier.narrative:
The origin is documented to the appropriation. LTG Ronald L. Burgess Jr., Director of DIA, wrote to the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics in an info memo dated 3 December 2010 (U-10-2552/CE) that "The Advanced Aerospace Threat Identification Program was first sponsored in the Fiscal Year (FY) 2008 Defense Supplemental Appropriation Act by Senators Reid and Inouye with a $10 million add," for the purpose of investigating "foreign advanced aerospace weapon threats from the present out to the next 40 years" and to "build an infrastructure to house a center of expertise on advanced aerospace technologies." The FY2010 Defense Appropriations Act added $12 million more. DIA issued an RFP naming twelve technical areas: lift, propulsion, control, armament, signatures reduction, materials, configuration, power generation, temporal translation, human effects, human interface, and technology integration. The contract went to BAASS, which Burgess notes was "the only bid." A separate DHS memo dated 28 November 2011 puts the two-year total at $22M, the deliverables at 38 research papers, and describes "an active, searchable database (now with greater than 100,000+ entries)."

The procurement history in that DHS memo adds names the DoD record does not volunteer. In May 2008 Senators Reid, Inouye and Stevens invited a DIA program manager (name redacted in the release) to meet with them about a research program involving 'exotic sciences.' In July 2008 LTG Michael Maples, then Director of DIA, was briefed by Reid directly. The redacted program manager is widely identified in secondary literature as James Lacatski; the released document does not name him.

The Reid letter of 24 June 2009 to Deputy Secretary William Lynn III is the load-bearing artifact. Reid asks for a Restricted SAP with a Bigoted Access List for specific portions of AATIP, and enumerates what needs protecting. First, "The methodology used to identify, acquire, study, and engineer the advanced technologies associated with AATIP." Second, allocation of personnel, support and oversight, because "Protection of industry partnerships and participation is critical. Public awareness of an industry's AATIP affiliation may discourage that industry's further participation with the U.S. Government in this program." Third, "Application and engineering" — where Reid writes that "The nuanced manner in which some of these technologies will be collected, engineered and applied by the U.S. may require senior level government approval" and that access to "the 'big picture' or overall intent of the program" should be restricted to a strict Bigoted List. Attachment 1 to the letter designates SAP Category "Intelligence, DoD Acquisition," program length FY09-FY13, and lists a preliminary bigoted list beginning with Lynn, Reid, Inouye, and Robert T. Herbert of the U.S. Senate; the contractor list begins with BAASS.

DIA said no. Burgess writes that in November 2009, at the request of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence, DIA reviewed the program and "determined that, based on classification levels of current and projected deliverables, insufficient grounds existed to classify the program, invoke an ACCM, or establish a restricted SAP." He and Lynn then met Reid in November 2009, "determined the reports were of limited value to DIA," and Burgess suggested transition to another agency. That is the documented push that lands at DHS as KONA BLUE in 2011.

The second life of the name begins in 2017. On 16 December 2017 the New York Times identified AATIP and Luis Elizondo, who had resigned from OUSD(I) effective 4 October 2017. From 2019 onward Pentagon spokeswoman Susan Gough has said Elizondo "had no assigned responsibilities for AATIP." In August 2024, after a three-year FOIA fight, The Black Vault obtained a 2017 draft memorandum authored by Elizondo and intended for issuance by Deputy Secretary Patrick Shanahan. The memo describes AATIP's strategic focus as "beyond next generation technologies in the areas of lift, propulsion, cloaking, and human effects," states that "DoD continues to consider AATIP a priority," and directs that "all DoD elements are hereby required to provide a courtesy copy of any data and information obtained from the field that related to unexplained or unknown aerial systems to the Director of Defense Intelligence for Technical Collection and Special Programs" — the position then held by Neill Tipton. DoD had told The Black Vault in December 2021 that no such records existed.

Who matters by name: Reid, Inouye, Stevens; Robert T. Herbert (Reid staff); Lynn; Maples; Burgess; Lacatski (per secondary sourcing); Robert Bigelow and BAASS; Hal Puthoff and Eric Davis as DIRD authors; Elizondo; Tipton; Shanahan; Gough. The record shows an earmarked, contractor-executed technology-exploitation effort whose sponsor asked in writing for engineering-grade compartmentation and was refused. The record does not show DIA ever taking custody of physical material under this contract, and does not resolve whether the OUSD(I) 'AATIP' Elizondo describes was the same activity or a successor riding the same nickname.

entityDossier.whatItIs: KONA BLUE was an unacknowledged, waived Prospective Special Access Program established inside the Department of Homeland Security Science and Technology Directorate by Under Secretary Dr. Tara O'Toole on 11 July 2011, and terminated by Deputy Secretary Jane Holl Lute effective 10 February 2012. Its stated purpose was "to investigate, identify and potentially exploit sensitive advanced aerospace-related technology and to prevent disclosure of scientific, technical and engineering data vital to the US." It was the direct successor proposal to the DIA AAWSAP/AATIP contract and was to be funded by a congressional add steered by Senators Reid and Lieberman.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: KONA BLUE is the best-documented attempt in the modern record to build a compartmented U.S. government home for exploitation of materials of claimed non-human origin, and the government declassified the paperwork itself in 2023-2024. The program's own approval memo states DHS proposed a SAP because "we have been informed that there is a body of previous work held by other entities that requires a SAP level classification to access it." That sentence is an admission, in a signed DHS action memo, that someone told the Under Secretary for Science and Technology that SAP-protected prior work existed and was held elsewhere. AARO's cover narrative asserts that interviewees identified KONA BLUE as "a Department of Homeland Security (DHS) sensitive compartment established to protect the retrieval and exploitation of 'non-human biologics'" and then argues the program never got materials because it was never approved. Both can be true and the interesting question survives: who were the "other entities," and what was the "body of previous work"? The termination reason of record is not that the claims were false. Deputy Secretary Lute killed it over adequacy of threat/vulnerability justification and insufficiency of budget and personnel documentation.
entityDossier.narrative:
The declassified package released jointly by DoD and DHS is unusually complete: an establishment memo, a decision briefing, SAPOC minutes, an action memo, a termination memo, a memorandum for the record, and — folded into the same release — the underlying Reid letter and DIA info memo that explain where the program came from.

Establishment: on 11 July 2011 the Director of DHS S&T's Special Projects Office asked Dr. Tara O'Toole, Under Secretary for Science and Technology and an Original Classification Authority, to approve creation of KONA BLUE as a Prospective Special Access Program under DHS Instruction 140-04-001. The stated purpose was "to investigate, identify and analyze sensitive advanced materials and technologies and to assess potential emerging and/or disruptive scientific and technical data necessary in support of national security." O'Toole approved. Classification was TOP SECRET//KONA BLUE//NOFORN, HANDLE VIA SPECIAL ACCESS CHANNELS ONLY, classified under E.O. reason 1.4(e), with a declassification date of 25 April 2036. The DHS SAPCO decision briefing lists the program manager as Joel Wall, S&T Special Programs Division.

Scope: the proposal document describes four research centers — Data Collection and Analysis, Advanced Technology, Consciousness, and Technology Application/Integration — investigating "emerging and/or disruptive advanced materials and controls, alternative energy/power source/generation opportunities, temporal translation; human effects and interface, signature reduction and weaponry, as well as technology integration." That is the AAWSAP twelve-area list with a Consciousness Center bolted on. The Department's interest area is stated as "the scientific and technical investigation, threat analysis, and assessment of materials and data of unique origin, engineering, and purpose." Materials of unique origin. Written by DHS.

Money: the planned research objectives slide gives FY12 $12M, FY13 $25M, FY14 $35-50M, FY15-FY18 TBD. The SAPCO briefing gives "Expected amount for funding expected to be 12 to 15m" and flags a pending issue: a "Classified Line Item in CSO budget" and that the Under Secretary for Management "has concurred in the need to establish a Business/Administrative SAP to handle primarily 'unacknowledged' monies (e.g., KONA BLUE)." A dedicated financial vehicle for unacknowledged money was being stood up to receive it.

The politics are in the SAPOC minutes of 21 November 2011, chaired by Deputy Secretary Jane Holl Lute, with Caryn Wagner (U/S Intelligence and Analysis), Rafael Borras (U/S Management), Ivan Fong (General Counsel), Gregory Marshall (Chief Security Officer), Steven J. Cover (Chief SAPCO), security officers Michael Zawasky and Allen Olsen, and O'Toole. The minutes record that "The Deputy Secretary opened the meeting with an explanation of what caused this meeting to occur with some sense of urgency which was the impending transfer of funds to DHS from Senators Reid and Leiberman to conduct the KONA BLUE program." O'Toole "stated that the Senators were prepared to provide $10M for the execution of this program in the FY12 budget." She was asked why the FBI was not approached and answered that the FBI "had no organic capability to do research & development in the scientific arena." Wagner raised whether S&T even had collection authority, and whether KONA BLUE "is actually an intelligence program which DIA no longer had the authority to conduct per Executive Order 12333." Lute closed by tasking O'Toole and Cover with a 5-10 page paper documenting "how we got to where we are now with the KONA BLUE program, it's provenance (history) while at DIA, and exactly what science would be researched," adding that "S2 is still not certain of what the 'It' is in the program or otherwise what exactly we are researching."

The November action memo from O'Toole records that in October 2011 she met with Senator Lieberman, Chairman of Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and Senate Majority Leader Reid, to discuss program funding. It also states the operative custody claim: "A SAP is proposed as we have been informed that there is a body of previous work held by other entities that requires a SAP level classification to access it."

Death: a progress review was held 8 December 2011 in Lute's office with Fong, Wagner, Cover and Associate General Counsel Kronisch. O'Toole was invited but could not attend. Lute directed immediate termination. The termination memo is dated 12 December 2011 and Lute's signature block shows Disapprove dated 2-10-12. DHS's Acting Deputy Secretary Kristie Canegallo confirmed in a 5 February 2024 letter to Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks that the PSAP was "terminated on February 10, 2012." A memorandum for the record from Cover dated 5 June 2013 states that no security classification guide, SOP, facility accreditation or AIS plan was ever issued, that all briefed personnel would be administratively debriefed, and that "No other documentation or paperwork would be required."

AARO's framing, published in 2024, is that KONA BLUE "never received any materials or funding" and that "no data or material of any kind was ever transferred to or collected by DHS under the auspices of KONA BLUE." On the narrow question of DHS custody, the paperwork supports that. On the broader question the AARO narrative raises and does not answer: DHS believed material would be delivered, and DHS wrote that a body of prior work was held by other entities under SAP protection. AARO does not identify those entities.

Norquist on 4 August 2020 and announced publicly on 14 August 2020, led by the Department of the Navy under the cognizance of the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security. Its stated mission was to detect, analyze and catalog UAP that could potentially pose a threat to U.S. national security. It produced the dataset behind the June 2021 ODNI preliminary assessment and was superseded in November 2021 by AOIMSG and in 2022 by AARO.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: The UAPTF is where the modern disclosure fight acquired its documents and its witnesses. David Grusch served as the National Reconnaissance Office representative to the UAPTF, and it was from inside that role that he says he was briefed on, and then denied access to, a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering program. That is the specific institutional pathway by which a legacy program's existence leaked into a body that Congress could subpoena. The task force also demonstrates the concealment mechanism in miniature: a Navy-led, OUSD(I&S)-supervised body with an unclassified public face and a classified annex, stood up only after decades of the same phenomena being handled through channels Congress was not shown. Within fifteen months of its public announcement it was dissolved and its functions moved twice, each time into a differently named organization with different reporting lines. Reorganization is a documented concealment technique on this board, and the UAPTF-to-AOIMSG-to-AARO chain is the cleanest recent example of it.
entityDossier.narrative:
The establishment is on the record and unambiguous. The Navy's own press release of 14 August 2020 states: "On Aug. 4, 2020, Deputy Secretary of Defense David L. Norquist approved the establishment of an Unidentified Aerial Phenomena (UAP) Task Force (UAPTF). The Department of the Navy, under the cognizance of the Office of the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security, will lead the UAPTF." The mission statement is "to detect, analyze and catalog UAPs that could potentially pose a threat to U.S. national security." Note what is absent: any reference to materials, recoveries, or prior programs. The public charter is a sensor-and-safety charter.

What the UAPTF actually produced was the dataset in the ODNI preliminary assessment delivered 25 June 2021, prepared in response to a reporting provision attached to the Intelligence Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2021. That nine-page unclassified assessment, with a classified annex, covers 144 reports from U.S. government sources between November 2004 and March 2021, states that most reports came from Navy and other military aviators, and identifies a small number of cases where UAP "appeared to remain stationary in winds aloft, move against the wind, maneuver abruptly, or move at considerable speed, without discernable means of propulsion." The assessment explicitly declines to attribute the phenomena and cites limited, inconsistent reporting as the principal analytic constraint. It is the government's own written acknowledgment that a body of unexplained aerospace observations exists inside its own sensor record.

The personnel question is where the task force becomes load-bearing for the program argument. David Grusch, an Air Force veteran and intelligence officer, served as the NRO representative to the UAPTF from 2019 to 2021 and then as his agency's co-lead for UAP and trans-medium object analysis at the National Geospatial-Intelligence Agency from 2021 to 2023. In 2022 he filed a complaint with the Intelligence Community Inspector General that was found credible and urgent for reporting to the congressional intelligence committees. On 26 July 2023, under oath before the House Oversight Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, Grusch testified that in the course of his official duties he was informed of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering program to which he was denied access, and that recoveries included non-human biologics. Whatever one concludes about the substance, the provenance is institutional: the claim entered the public record through a person whose job was to represent a national intelligence agency to a DoD task force.

The dissolution is as instructive as the founding. On 23 November 2021 Deputy Secretary of Defense Kathleen Hicks, in coordination with the Director of National Intelligence, directed the Under Secretary of Defense for Intelligence and Security to establish the Airborne Object Identification and Management Synchronization Group as the successor to the Navy's UAPTF, with oversight from an Airborne Object Identification and Management Executive Council drawn from DoD and the intelligence community. Ronald Moultrie was the USD(I&S) of record. AOIMSG itself lasted months before being reconstituted in July 2022 as the All-domain Anomaly Resolution Office. Three names, three charters, three sets of reporting relationships, in under two years, for the same subject matter. Each transition reset what Congress had been briefed on and who owed the briefing.

The naming precision matters here in the same way it matters for AATIP. The UAPTF was a Navy-led DoD task force with an OUSD(I&S) reporting chain. It was not a special access program, it did not have acquisition authority, and nothing in its public charter gives it custody of anything. That is precisely Grusch's point: he says the compartmented activity he learned about was adjacent to, and walled off from, the body Congress had been told was handling the subject. The UAPTF is therefore best read on this board not as the program but as the sensor that detected the program from inside the building.

Who matters by name: Norquist (approving authority), Hicks (dissolving authority), Moultrie (USD(I&S)), Grusch (NRO representative), and the ODNI and Navy officials who signed out the June 2021 assessment. What the record shows is a legitimate, publicly chartered analytic body producing a public product that concedes unexplained observations. What the record does not show is any UAPTF authority over, or access to, materials — and the absence of that authority in a body specifically created to be the government's answer on UAP is the anomaly worth pulling on.

Three hearings define the record.

On 26 July 2023 the Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs, chaired by Rep. The witnesses were Ryan Graves, Executive Director of Americans for Safe Aerospace; Commander David Fravor, former commanding officer of the Black Aces squadron; and David Grusch, former National Reconnaissance Office representative to the UAP Task Force. Grusch testified under oath that in the course of his official duties he was informed of a multi-decade crash retrieval and reverse-engineering program to which he was denied access, that he had interviewed dozens of witnesses over several years, and that recoveries included non-human biologics, repeatedly stating he could provide specifics in a secure setting. Fravor described the November 2004 Nimitz encounter. Graves testified on reporting stigma and aviation safety. It was the first time a sworn witness told a House committee, on camera, that the United States operates a concealed retrieval program.

On 13 November 2024 the Subcommittee on Cybersecurity, Information Technology, and Government Innovation and the Subcommittee on National Security, the Border, and Foreign Affairs held a joint hearing, 'Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena: Exposing the Truth.' The full transcript was published as HHRG-118-GO12-Transcript-20241113 and the hearing was printed as CHRG-118hhrg57440. The composition of the witness panel is itself notable: a retired flag officer, a former NASA associate administrator, a former DoD official, and a journalist, three of whom held senior federal positions.

Anna Paulina Luna, held 'Restoring Public Trust Through UAP Transparency and Whistleblower Protection' in HVC-210. entityDossier.whatItIs: The Status Reports are a series of seven self-published monographs by Cincinnati ufologist Leonard H. Stringfield (1920-1994), issued between 1978 and 1994, compiling anonymized first- and second-hand accounts of alleged U.S. military recoveries of crashed craft and occupant bodies. The first, 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A Case Study of Alleged UFOs and Occupants in Military Custody,' was presented at the Ninth Annual MUFON Symposium in Dayton, Ohio in July 1978. The series is the foundational corpus of the modern crash-retrieval literature.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: Every modern claim about a legacy retrieval program is downstream of a source pool that Stringfield assembled first. His method — solicit military and medical personnel, strip identities, publish coded case abstracts — created a body of testimony in the late 1970s and 1980s whose content is structurally identical to what witnesses told the House Oversight Committee in 2023 and 2024: recovery of intact and damaged craft, transport to secure facilities, autopsy of non-human remains, compartmented handling outside normal channels. If those 2023 claims are a modern fabrication, the fabrication is forty-five years old and was published in monograph form by a MUFON public relations director with a documented Air Defense Command reporting relationship. If they are not, Stringfield's files are the earliest systematic index of the program's personnel. Either way, the corpus is a testable object: the sources are anonymous, but the cases carry dates, units and installations, and the underlying files exist as a physical archive. The honest tier here is low on the substance and high on the provenance.
entityDossier.narrative:
Stringfield's standing rests on a career that predates the crash-retrieval work by two decades. In 1954 he founded Civilian Research, Interplanetary Flying Objects (CRIFO) in Cincinnati and published the newsletter ORBIT. He wrote 'Inside Saucer Post...3-0 Blue: CRIFO Views the Status Quo' in 1957, the same year he became public relations adviser to Donald Keyhoe's National Investigations Committee on Aerial Phenomena. From 1967 to 1969 he served as an 'Early Warning Coordinator' for the Condon Committee at the University of Colorado, screening incoming reports for possible scientific study. He was later Director of Public Relations for the Mutual UFO Network. His day job, throughout, was Director of Public Relations and Marketing Services for DuBois Chemicals, a division of Chemed Corporation. He died of lung cancer on 18 December 1994.

The relevant biographical detail for a concealment analysis is the reporting arrangement. NICAP's own biography states that Stringfield worked in cooperation with the U.S. Air Force from 1953 to 1957 investigating and reporting UFO activity, having been assigned a special code number for reporting to the Air Defense Command in Columbus, Ohio. A civilian researcher holding an assigned reporting code to ADC is an unusual artifact and it explains why military personnel later approached him rather than a journalist.

The Status Report series, with titles and dates as published: Status Report I, 'Retrievals of the Third Kind: A case study of alleged UFOs and occupants in military custody' (1978, from the Ninth Annual MUFON Symposium, Dayton, Ohio, July 1978); Status Report II, 'The UFO Crash/Retrieval Syndrome: New Sources, New Data' (1980); Status Report III, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Amassing the Evidence' (1982); Status Report IV, 'The fatal encounter at Ft. Dix-McGuire: A case study' (1985); Status Report V, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Is the coverup lid lifting?' (1989); Status Report VI, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: The Inner Sanctum' (1991); Status Report VII, 'UFO Crash/Retrievals: Search for Proof in a Hall of Mirrors' (1994). All were self-published. A 2019 compilation reissued all seven in one volume.

The method is the weakness and also the reason the corpus is worth auditing. Stringfield presented cases as numbered abstracts summarizing accounts from unnamed informants, most described as military or medical personnel. Some abstracts are explicitly composites; the widely cited 'Abstract XXII: Biological data relating to retrieved alien bodies' is described as a composite assembled from anonymous medical and military sources. No abstract in the published series can be independently verified from the text alone, because the text withholds the identifying information that would permit verification. That is a disqualifying defect for any individual claim and simultaneously the exact behavior one would expect from a researcher protecting serving personnel.

Status Report IV is the outlier and the best single entry point for an analyst. It abandons the abstract format for a single named case study, the alleged January 1978 incident at Fort Dix and McGuire Air Force Base in New Jersey, with a specific installation, a specific date window, and identifiable military police and security police units. That case is checkable against Army and Air Force records in a way the composite abstracts are not.

The physical archive survives. MUFON's Project Aquarius Library lists the Stringfield Files as a private collection. The underlying correspondence, informant notes and case files in that collection are the actual evidentiary object; the published monographs are only the redacted output. Whether the collection contains unredacted informant identities is the single most consequential unanswered question about this entity.

What the record shows: a well-documented researcher with an unusual official reporting relationship who, over sixteen years, published seven monographs compiling anonymous military testimony about recoveries and autopsies, and who left an archive. What the record does not show: any named source, any document, any physical item, or any independent corroboration of a single abstract. Tiered honestly, the existence, authorship, dating and archival survival of the Status Reports are Tier 1 or 2; every substantive claim inside them is Tier 3 pending identification of sources.

entityDossier.whatItIs: The ADAM Research Project — Acquisition and Data Analysis of Materials — is a private materials-analysis program launched in July 2018 by To The Stars Academy of Arts & Science, a Delaware public benefit corporation founded by Tom DeLonge. It acquires physical samples reportedly recovered from advanced aerospace vehicles of unknown origin and contracts laboratory analysis, principally through Hal Puthoff's EarthTech International in Austin, Texas. Its best-known holding is the magnesium-zinc-bismuth 'Art's Parts' sample purchased with an archive from journalist Linda Moulton Howe in July 2019.
entityDossier.whyImplicated: ADAM is the only publicly documented instance of claimed recovered material moving from private custody into a federal laboratory pipeline with a signed government agreement attached. In October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command covering material science, space-time metric engineering, beamed energy propulsion and active camouflage. By 2024 the same magnesium-zinc-bismuth sample had been analyzed at Oak Ridge National Laboratory with AARO in the room, and Puthoff and Eric Davis — both of whom authored deliverables under the DIA AAWSAP contract a decade earlier — wrote the private counter-analysis. That is a closed loop: the same physicists who wrote the government's exotic-propulsion reference documents in 2009-2010 are the ones adjudicating a national laboratory's findings on a claimed recovered artifact in 2024. Whether or not the sample is exotic, the custody chain and the recurrence of the same named individuals across government and private roles is the finding.
entityDossier.narrative:
TTSA announced ADAM in July 2018 as an academic research program focused on the collection and scientific evaluation of material samples obtained through reported encounters with advanced aerospace vehicles of unknown origin. Analysis was contracted to EarthTech International, the Austin think tank run by Dr. Harold E. Puthoff, who was simultaneously TTSA's Vice President of Science and Technology and had been a senior adviser and subcontractor on the DIA-funded AAWSAP/AATIP work.

The acquisition that gave ADAM an object rather than a concept came on 25 July 2019. TTSA's press release states that it 'has acquired multiple pieces of metamaterials and an archive of initial analysis and research for their controversial ADAM Research Project,' materials 'previously retained and studied by investigative journalist Linda Moulton Howe and are reported to have come from an advanced aerospace vehicle of unknown origin.' Steve Justice — TTSA's COO and formerly head of Advanced Systems at Lockheed Martin's Skunk Works — is quoted: 'The structure and composition of these materials are not from any known existing military or commercial application.' He adds the crucial custody caveat in the same paragraph: 'They've been collected from sources with varying levels of chain-of-custody documentation, so we are focusing on verifiable facts and working to develop independent scientific proof of the materials' properties and attributes.' And a dating claim: 'In some cases, the manufacturing technology required to fabricate the material is only now becoming available, but the material has been in documented possession since the mid-1990's.' Justice explicitly frames the endgame as transition to capability: 'If the claims associated with these assets can be validated and substantiated, then we can initiate work to transition them from being a technology to commercial and military capabilities.'

On 17 October 2019 TTSA announced a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement with the U.S. Army Combat Capabilities Development Command, sharing its work with the Ground Vehicle Systems Center and Ground Vehicle Survivability and Protection, with the Army providing laboratories, expertise and resources. The announced technology areas were material science, space-time metric engineering, quantum physics, beamed energy propulsion, and active camouflage. A CRADA is not a procurement; no money moved to TTSA and the Army acquired nothing. What it did establish is a formal, signed channel through which privately held claimed-exotic material could reach Army laboratories.

The analytic endgame arrived in 2024. Oak Ridge National Laboratory analyzed the magnesium-zinc-bismuth 'Art's Parts' sample; TTS posted the ORNL report in July of that year. A TTS-AARO-ORNL meeting was held on 27 August 2024. Puthoff and Eric W. Davis then produced their own analysis, submitted to the TTS Board of Directors on 27 September 2024 and published by TTS with a recommendation history attached. TTS's own summary of the outcome is unusually candid and is the single most useful sentence ADAM has produced: 'the Puthoff/Davis analysis (and the ORNL analysis) did not reveal any form of proof of exotic (Extraterrestrial, Ultra-terrestrial, or inter-dimensional) origin, but it did not absolutely rule it out either.' TTS adds that 'the actual purpose of the material, though clearly manufactured, still remains a bit of a mystery.'

AARO's 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1 states more bluntly that a piece of metal alleged to be recovered from an off-world spacecraft was determined to be ordinary, of terrestrial origin, and to possess no exceptional qualities. Both statements can be reconciled: nothing exotic was demonstrated. What was demonstrated is process — a private entity holding claimed recovered material got it into a DOE national laboratory and into a room with the Pentagon's UAP office.

The scientific parallel track matters for method rather than result. Garry Nolan of Stanford, Jacques Vallée, Sizun Jiang and Larry Lemke published 'Improved instrumental techniques, including isotopic analysis, applicable to the characterization of unusual materials with potential relevance to aerospace forensics' in Progress in Aerospace Sciences volume 128 in January 2022, DOI 10.1016/j.paerosci.2021.100788. That paper is the peer-reviewed statement of what a defensible analysis of a claimed anomalous sample would look like — isotopic ratio analysis, SIMS, and comparison against known terrestrial baselines — and it is the standard against which every ADAM claim should be measured.

Who matters by name: Tom DeLonge (founder), Steve Justice (COO, ex-Skunk Works Advanced Systems), Hal Puthoff (EarthTech, TTSA VP Science and Technology, AAWSAP DIRD author), Eric W. Davis (AAWSAP DIRD author, co-author of the 2024 counter-analysis), Linda Moulton Howe (prior custodian), Luis Elizondo and Chris Mellon (TTSA principals in the founding period), Garry Nolan and Jacques Vallée on the independent scientific track. What the record shows is a documented chain of private acquisition, a signed Army CRADA, a national-laboratory analysis, and a published negative-but-not-exclusionary result. What the record does not show is any chain of custody back to a recovery event.

entityDossier.denialPosture: AARO's public position, in its 2024 Historical Record Report Volume 1, is that a sample alleged to be from an off-world craft was found to be ordinary and terrestrial with no exceptional qualities. Notably, TTS itself does not dispute the negative finding; its published position is that neither ORNL nor its own analysts proved exotic origin, only that they did not absolutely rule it out. There is no live factual dispute over the ORNL result — the dispute is over interpretation of manufacture, purpose and provenance.
connections: Hal Puthoff and Eric W. Davis authored Defense Intelligence Reference Documents under the DIA AAWSAP/AATIP contract and then produced the private counter-analysis of the ORNL findings in 2024. The same two names span the government exotic-propulsion literature and the private materials custody effort.
EarthTech International is the connective tissue between AATIP-era government work and ADAM-era private analysis.
Steve Justice carries Lockheed Martin Skunk Works Advanced Systems provenance directly into the materials-custody claim, one of the few documented senior primes-to-private transitions in this space.
The October 2019 Army CCDC CRADA is the only signed federal instrument publicly attached to claimed recovered material; the Ground Vehicle Systems Center is the named federal counterparty.
Oak Ridge National Laboratory is the DOE facility of record for the analysis, putting a national laboratory in the custody chain.
AARO participated in the 27 August 2024 TTS-ORNL meeting, meaning the Pentagon's UAP office is a documented party to a private materials analysis.
Linda Moulton Howe is the prior custodian and the origin of the 'Art's Parts' chain, which traces to the Art Bell radio program in the mid-1990s.
Garry Nolan and Jacques Vallée provide the peer-reviewed methodological standard and are the independent scientific track against which ADAM's claims should be judged.

The Schumer-Rounds eminent domain provision, stripped from the final FY2024 NDAA, would have compelled federal seizure of exactly the class of privately held material ADAM holds; its removal left ADAM's holdings in private hands.
